arXiv:2603.05540v1 [cs.CL] 04 Mar 2026

Attention Meets Reachability: Structural Equivalence and Efficiency
in Grammar-Constrained LLM Decoding

Faruk Alpay Department of Computer Engineering, Bahçeşehir University, Istanbul, Turkey faruk.alpay@bahcesehir.edu.tr   Bilge Senturk Department of Industrial Engineering, Bahçeşehir University, Istanbul, Turkey bilge.senturk@bahcesehir.edu.tr
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Grammar-constrained decoding (GCD) enforces that an autoregressive language model generates outputs within a formal language specified by a context-free grammar (CFG). We formalize GCD as a coupling between a Transformer-style next-token distribution and a reachability oracle over a pushdown system compiled from a CFG, and develop a unified theoretical framework addressing both the complexity structure of the constraint engine and the probabilistic fidelity of the constrained generator. We prove an oracle invariance theorem: language-equivalent grammars induce identical next-token admissibility sets for every prefix (hence identical logit masks), yet can yield provably different compiled state spaces and online ambiguity costs. We give exact state-count blowups for the canonical an​bna^{n}b^{n} language under redundant nonterminal delegation, and introduce a left-to-right structural ambiguity cost (SAC) that measures incremental packed-parse-forest growth per token. For two equivalent Σ∗\Sigma^{*} grammars, we prove that SAC is O⁡(1)O(1) per token under right-recursion but Θ⁡(t2)\Theta(t^{2}) per token (and Θ⁡(n3)\Theta(n^{3}) cumulatively) under concatenation, via tight bounds on packed parse forest density. Beyond asymptotic complexity, we establish three further theoretical contributions. First, we elevate SAC into engine-independent lower bounds: any sound, retrieval-efficient, parse-preserving online masking engine must incur Ω⁡(t2)\Omega(t^{2}) work per token (and Ω⁡(n3)\Omega(n^{3}) cumulatively) on a specific constant-size CFG family; this parallels classical complexity results connecting CFG parsing to matrix multiplication [34, 18]. Second, we define decoding-cost equivalence classes of grammars and prove the existence of minimal-SAC representatives within bounded rewrite families, clarifying what canonical low-SAC normal forms can and cannot mean. Third, we formalize grammar-conditioned autoregressive processes: the true conditional sampler p(⋅∣τ(y)∈L)p(\cdot\mid\tau(y)\in L) is characterized by a Doob hh-transform, and we prove sharp distortion bounds for hard-masked decoding in terms of survival-probability spread among admissible next tokens. Finally, we integrate these results with Transformer and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, derive decoding-time latency envelopes in terms of vocabulary size, active state sets, and beam width, and extend SAC into a measurement-calibrated predictive performance model that supports empirical validation and automated grammar optimization.

1 Introduction

Autoregressive large language models (LLMs) define distributions of the form

pθ(y1:T)=∏t=1Tpθ(yt∣y<t),p_{\theta}(y_{1:T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}), (1)

where yt∈𝒱y_{t}\in\mathcal{V} is a vocabulary token and θ\theta are model parameters. In many deployments, however, the desired output is not arbitrary text but a structured artifact (e.g., SQL, JSON, or a programming language fragment). Grammar-constrained decoding (GCD) addresses this by restricting generation to tokens that keep the current prefix completable under a formal language specification, typically a CFG, rejecting inadmissible tokens on the fly [28, 2]. The same conceptual interface underlies popular open-source toolchains for structured generation [19, 13, 8, 36, 15].

This paper addresses a tension at the core of GCD: language equivalence is semantic (two grammars that generate the same strings are interchangeable from the user’s perspective), but constrained decoding executes a specific compiled recognizer whose runtime depends on grammar structure. Our central claim is that even when two CFGs generate exactly the same language, they can induce radically different internal search spaces for a left-to-right decoding engine. This discrepancy is not semantic; it is purely structural, and it manifests through pushdown reachability.

Contributions.

We make six main contributions.

  1. 1.

    Pushdown reachability formalization. We formalize GCD as a coupling between a neural model and a pushdown reachability oracle, grounding the decoding step in CFL parsing and reachability theory [16, 9, 27, 4]. We prove oracle invariance under language equivalence and give an exact algebraic account of hard-masked decoding.

  2. 2.

    State-space blowup bounds. We prove exact control-state blowup counts for the an​bna^{n}b^{n} language under redundant nonterminal delegation, giving a concrete, mechanically checkable notion of “engine state space inflation.”

  3. 3.

    Structural ambiguity cost (SAC) and tight growth bounds. We introduce SAC as a left-to-right per-token measure of packed-parse-forest growth. We prove that SAC\mathrm{SAC} is Θ⁡(t2)\Theta(t^{2}) per token (Θ⁡(n3)\Theta(n^{3}) cumulative) for a concatenative Σ∗\Sigma^{*} grammar and O⁡(1)O(1) for an equivalent right-recursive one.

  4. 4.

    Engine-independent lower bounds. We define a parse-preserving, retrieval-efficient masking engine model and prove that any such engine must incur Ω⁡(t2)\Omega(t^{2}) work per token on a constant-size CFG family, making the SAC lower bound unconditional within this semantic interface. This is complementary to—but distinct from—Valiant/Lee-style reductions [34, 18].

  5. 5.

    Decoding-cost equivalence classes and canonical low-SAC forms. We define ≡dec\equiv_{\mathrm{dec}} as joint language and SAC equivalence, and prove that minimal-SAC grammar representatives exist within any finite bounded-rewrite family.

  6. 6.

    Grammar-conditioned autoregressive processes. We characterize the true conditional sampler p(⋅∣τ(y)∈L)p(\cdot\mid\tau(y)\in L) via a Doob hh-transform and derive sharp one-step KL and total-variation distortion bounds for hard-masked decoding in terms of the survival-probability spread among admissible tokens.

We additionally derive algebraic constraints describing how the reachability-valid transition subset modulates Transformer logits and MoE routing [35, 30, 10], and show how SAC can be operationalized into a predictive performance model calibrated against empirical traces from real inference stacks [12, 6, 5].

2 Decoding as Pushdown Reachability

We fix (i) a CFG over an abstract terminal alphabet, (ii) a tokenizer mapping from model tokens to terminal strings, and (iii) an explicit compilation of the CFG to a pushdown automaton whose reachable configuration set determines admissible next tokens.

2.1 Languages, prefixes, and tokenization

Definition 1 (CFG).

A context-free grammar is a tuple G=(N,Σ,P,S)G=(N,\Sigma,P,S) where NN is a finite set of nonterminals, Σ\Sigma is a finite set of terminals, P⊆N×(N∪Σ)∗P\subseteq N\times(N\cup\Sigma)^{*} is a finite set of productions written A→αA\to\alpha, and S∈NS\in N is the start symbol. The language generated by GG is denoted ℒ⁡(G)⊆Σ∗\mathcal{L}(G)\subseteq\Sigma^{*}.

Definition 2 (Prefix closure and one-step extension).

For any language L⊆Σ∗L\subseteq\Sigma^{*}, define its prefix closure

Pref⁡(L)≔{u∈Σ∗:∃v∈Σ∗​ such that ​u​v∈L}.\operatorname{Pref}(L)\coloneqq\{u\in\Sigma^{*}\;:\;\exists v\in\Sigma^{*}\text{ such that }uv\in L\}.

Define the next-terminal set after prefix uu as

NextL⁡(u)≔{a∈Σ:u​a∈Pref⁡(L)}.\operatorname{Next}_{L}(u)\coloneqq\{a\in\Sigma\;:\;ua\in\operatorname{Pref}(L)\}.

Define the end signal ⟨eos⟩\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle as admissible after uu iff u∈Lu\in L.

Definition 3 (Tokenizer homomorphism).

Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} be the LLM vocabulary. A tokenizer homomorphism is a map τ:𝒱→Σ∗\tau:\mathcal{V}\to\Sigma^{*}. For a token sequence y1:T∈𝒱Ty_{1:T}\in\mathcal{V}^{T}, define its realized terminal string as

τ(y1:T)≔τ(y1)τ(y2)⋯τ(yT)∈Σ∗,\tau(y_{1:T})\coloneqq\tau(y_{1})\tau(y_{2})\cdots\tau(y_{T})\in\Sigma^{*},

where juxtaposition denotes concatenation in Σ∗\Sigma^{*}. We set τ⁡(⟨eos⟩)=ε\tau(\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle)=\varepsilon.

The constraint “the model output is in ℒ⁡(G)\mathcal{L}(G)” is interpreted as τ(y1:T)∈ℒ(G)\tau(y_{1:T})\in\mathcal{L}(G).

2.2 Pushdown automata and CFG compilation

Definition 4 (Nondeterministic PDA).

A nondeterministic pushdown automaton (NPDA) is a tuple

𝒜=(Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0,⊥,F),\mathcal{A}=(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,\delta,q_{0},\bot,F),

where QQ is a finite set of control states, Γ\Gamma is a finite stack alphabet with bottom marker ⊥\bot, q0∈Qq_{0}\in Q is the initial state, F⊆QF\subseteq Q is the set of accepting states, and

δ:Q×(Σ∪{ε})×Γ→𝒫⁡(Q×Γ∗)\delta:Q\times(\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\})\times\Gamma\to\mathcal{P}(Q\times\Gamma^{*})

is the transition function. A configuration is a triple (q,u,γ)(q,u,\gamma) where q∈Qq\in Q, u∈Σ∗u\in\Sigma^{*} is the unread input, and γ∈Γ∗\gamma\in\Gamma^{*} is the stack contents with ⊥\bot at the bottom. Acceptance is by final state with empty input and stack exactly ⊥\bot.

Definition 5 (Recursive-transition-network compilation).

Given G=(N,Σ,P,S)G=(N,\Sigma,P,S), define 𝒜G\mathcal{A}_{G} as follows. For each nonterminal A∈NA\in N, create control states qAinq_{A}^{\mathrm{in}} and qAoutq_{A}^{\mathrm{out}}. For each production p=(A→X1⋯Xm)∈Pp=(A\to X_{1}\cdots X_{m})\in P and each dot position i∈{0,1,…,m}i\in\{0,1,\dots,m\}, create a control state qp,iq_{p,i}. Let

Q≔{qstart}∪{qAin,qAout:A∈N}∪{qp,i:p∈P,i}.Q\coloneqq\{q_{\mathrm{start}}\}\cup\{q_{A}^{\mathrm{in}},q_{A}^{\mathrm{out}}:A\in N\}\cup\{q_{p,i}:p\in P,\,i\}.

Let the stack alphabet be Γ≔{⊥}∪{qp,i:p∈P,i}\Gamma\coloneqq\{\bot\}\cup\{q_{p,i}:p\in P,\,i\}. Define transitions:

  • •

    Start: δ(qstart,ε,⊥)∋(qSin,⊥)\delta(q_{\mathrm{start}},\varepsilon,\bot)\ni(q_{S}^{\mathrm{in}},\bot).

  • •

    Choice of production: for each production p=(A→⋯)p=(A\to\cdots), δ⁡(qAin,ε,γ)∋(qp,0,γ)\delta(q_{A}^{\mathrm{in}},\varepsilon,\gamma)\ni(q_{p,0},\gamma) for all γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma.

  • •

    Exit: δ⁡(qp,m,ε,γ)∋(qAout,γ)\delta(q_{p,m},\varepsilon,\gamma)\ni(q_{A}^{\mathrm{out}},\gamma).

  • •

    Terminals: if Xi∈ΣX_{i}\in\Sigma, then δ⁡(qp,i−1,Xi,γ)∋(qp,i,γ)\delta(q_{p,i-1},X_{i},\gamma)\ni(q_{p,i},\gamma).

  • •

    Nonterminal calls: if Xi=B∈NX_{i}=B\in N, then δ⁡(qp,i−1,ε,γ)∋(qBin,qp,i​γ)\delta(q_{p,i-1},\varepsilon,\gamma)\ni(q_{B}^{\mathrm{in}},q_{p,i}\gamma) and, for each return address r=qp,ir=q_{p,i}, δ⁡(qBout,ε,r)∋(r,ε)\delta(q_{B}^{\mathrm{out}},\varepsilon,r)\ni(r,\varepsilon).

Set q0=qstartq_{0}=q_{\mathrm{start}} and F={qSout}F=\{q_{S}^{\mathrm{out}}\}. We call QQ the engine control-state space.

Proposition 1 (Correctness of compilation).

For every CFG GG, the compiled NPDA 𝒜G\mathcal{A}_{G} accepts exactly ℒ⁡(G)\mathcal{L}(G).

Proof.

Each nonterminal invocation pushes a return address and transitions into the callee’s entry state; completing a nonterminal pops the return address and resumes at the caller’s dot-position state. Terminal transitions consume exactly the required terminal; nondeterminism models production choice. An accepting run corresponds to a leftmost derivation tree and vice versa. A detailed proof follows by adapting the classic CFG→\toPDA conversion in [16, Ch. 6] to the dot-position control-state representation. ∎

2.3 Engine semantics for left-to-right masking

Definition 6 (Reachability and liveness).

Fix a compiled NPDA 𝒜G\mathcal{A}_{G}. For a terminal prefix u∈Σ∗u\in\Sigma^{*}, define ReachG⁡(u)\operatorname{Reach}_{G}(u) as the set of configurations reachable from the initial configuration after consuming exactly uu, allowing any number of ε\varepsilon-moves before, between, and after terminal moves. A configuration cc is live if there exists some v∈Σ∗v\in\Sigma^{*} such that cc reaches an accepting configuration after consuming vv. Let CoReachG⁡(u)⊆ReachG⁡(u)\operatorname{CoReach}_{G}(u)\subseteq\operatorname{Reach}_{G}(u) be the subset of reachable configurations that are live.

Definition 7 (Admissible next vocabulary tokens).

Given prefix u∈Σ∗u\in\Sigma^{*}, define the admissible token set

ΩG​(u)≔{v∈𝒱:CoReachG⁡(u​τ​(v))≠∅}.\Omega_{G}(u)\coloneqq\{v\in\mathcal{V}\;:\;\operatorname{CoReach}_{G}(u\,\tau(v))\neq\emptyset\}.
Remark 1 (Reachability as the computational bottleneck).

Computing CoReachG\operatorname{CoReach}_{G} is a reachability question in a pushdown system, tightly connected to CFL reachability and interprocedural analysis [27, 1, 4]. Modern GCD implementations reduce this cost via offline preprocessing, memoization, deterministic pushdown compilation, and careful tokenizer alignment [2, 23, 6, 33, 5].

3 Structural Equivalence, Masked Decoding, and Probability Constraints

3.1 Oracle invariance under language equivalence

Definition 8 (Language equivalence).

Two CFGs GG and G′G^{\prime} are (strongly) equivalent if ℒ⁡(G)=ℒ⁡(G′)\mathcal{L}(G)=\mathcal{L}(G^{\prime}).

Theorem 1 (Oracle invariance).

If ℒ⁡(G)=ℒ⁡(G′)\mathcal{L}(G)=\mathcal{L}(G^{\prime}), then for every terminal prefix u∈Σ∗u\in\Sigma^{*},

ΩG​(u)=ΩG′​(u).\Omega_{G}(u)=\Omega_{G^{\prime}}(u).

Consequently, any decoding procedure that uses only the pair (pθ(⋅∣y<t),ΩG(τ(y<t)))(p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}),\,\Omega_{G}(\tau(y_{<t}))) is behaviorally invariant under replacing GG by G′G^{\prime}.

Proof.

Fix u∈Σ∗u\in\Sigma^{*} and v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V}. By definition, v∈ΩG​(u)v\in\Omega_{G}(u) iff CoReachG⁡(u​τ​(v))≠∅\operatorname{CoReach}_{G}(u\tau(v))\neq\emptyset. By correctness of compilation (Proposition 1), CoReachG⁡(w)≠∅\operatorname{CoReach}_{G}(w)\neq\emptyset iff w∈Pref⁡(ℒ⁡(G))w\in\operatorname{Pref}(\mathcal{L}(G)) (i.e., ww is completable). Thus

v∈ΩG​(u)⟺u​τ​(v)∈Pref⁡(ℒ⁡(G)).v\in\Omega_{G}(u)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ u\tau(v)\in\operatorname{Pref}(\mathcal{L}(G)).

Since ℒ⁡(G)=ℒ⁡(G′)\mathcal{L}(G)=\mathcal{L}(G^{\prime}) implies Pref⁡(ℒ⁡(G))=Pref⁡(ℒ⁡(G′))\operatorname{Pref}(\mathcal{L}(G))=\operatorname{Pref}(\mathcal{L}(G^{\prime})), the condition is identical for G′G^{\prime}. ∎

3.2 Masked decoding as a constrained stochastic process

Let ℓt∈ℝ|𝒱|\ell_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|} denote the model logits at step tt, with

pθ​(v∣y<t)=exp⁡(ℓt​(v))∑w∈𝒱exp⁡(ℓt​(w)).p_{\theta}(v\mid y_{<t})=\frac{\exp(\ell_{t}(v))}{\sum_{w\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(\ell_{t}(w))}.
Definition 9 (Hard mask operator).

Given A⊆𝒱A\subseteq\mathcal{V}, define mA∈(ℝ∪{−∞})|𝒱|m_{A}\in(\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\})^{|\mathcal{V}|} by

mA​(v)≔{0,v∈A,−∞,v∉A.m_{A}(v)\coloneqq\begin{cases}0,&v\in A,\\ -\infty,&v\notin A.\end{cases}

Define the masked next-token distribution

qθ,A​(v∣y<t)≔softmax⁡(ℓt+mA)​(v)=exp(ℓt(v))𝟏[v∈A]∑w∈Aexp⁡(ℓt​(w)).q_{\theta,A}(v\mid y_{<t})\coloneqq\mathrm{softmax}(\ell_{t}+m_{A})(v)=\frac{\exp(\ell_{t}(v))\mathbf{1}[v\in A]}{\sum_{w\in A}\exp(\ell_{t}(w))}.

In GCD, A=ΩG​(τ⁡(y<t))A=\Omega_{G}(\tau(y_{<t})). By Theorem 1, this depends only on the language, not on the grammar presentation.

Proposition 2 (Soundness of hard-masked decoding).

Let qθGq_{\theta}^{G} denote autoregressive sampling where at each step yt∼qθ,ΩG​(τ⁡(y<t))(⋅∣y<t)y_{t}\sim q_{\theta,\Omega_{G}(\tau(y_{<t}))}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}). Then every generated sample y1:Ty_{1:T} terminated by ⟨eos⟩\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle satisfies τ(y1:T)∈ℒ(G)\tau(y_{1:T})\in\mathcal{L}(G).

Proof.

At each step, the sampled token keeps the realized prefix in Pref⁡(ℒ⁡(G))\operatorname{Pref}(\mathcal{L}(G)). Moreover, ⟨eos⟩\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle is admissible only when the current realized prefix is in ℒ⁡(G)\mathcal{L}(G). Therefore termination implies membership. ∎

Remark 2 (Masking is not the true conditional distribution).

Sampling with hard masks yields a distribution supported on ℒ⁡(G)\mathcal{L}(G), but it is not in general equal to conditioning the base model on τ⁡(y)∈ℒ⁡(G)\tau(y)\in\mathcal{L}(G). Exact conditioning requires weighting by the model’s probability of eventual successful completion from each candidate next token. We characterize this discrepancy precisely via a Doob hh-transform in Section 8.

Lemma 1 (Separation from global conditioning).

There exist a base autoregressive model pθp_{\theta} and a language LL such that the masked process qθLq_{\theta}^{L} differs from the globally conditioned distribution pθ(⋅∣τ(y)∈L)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\tau(y)\in L).

Proof.

Let Σ={a,b}\Sigma=\{a,b\}, L={a,b​a}L=\{a,\,ba\}, and 𝒱={a,b,⟨eos⟩}\mathcal{V}=\{a,b,\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle\} with τ⁡(a)=a\tau(a)=a, τ⁡(b)=b\tau(b)=b, τ⁡(⟨eos⟩)=ε\tau(\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle)=\varepsilon. Set

pθ​(a∣ε)=0.6,pθ​(b∣ε)=0.4,pθ​(⟨eos⟩∣ε)=0,p_{\theta}(a\mid\varepsilon)=0.6,\quad p_{\theta}(b\mid\varepsilon)=0.4,\quad p_{\theta}(\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle\mid\varepsilon)=0,
pθ​(⟨eos⟩∣a)=0.1,pθ​(a∣a)=0.9,pθ​(b∣a)=0,p_{\theta}(\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle\mid a)=0.1,\quad p_{\theta}(a\mid a)=0.9,\quad p_{\theta}(b\mid a)=0,
pθ​(a∣b)=0.01,pθ​(b∣b)=0.99,pθ​(⟨eos⟩∣b)=0.p_{\theta}(a\mid b)=0.01,\quad p_{\theta}(b\mid b)=0.99,\quad p_{\theta}(\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle\mid b)=0.

Under the masked process, q⁡(b∣ε)=0.4q(b\mid\varepsilon)=0.4 (both tokens are admissible; mask unchanged at step 1). Under global conditioning, the total acceptance mass is

pθ​(accept via ​a)=0.6⋅0.1=0.06,pθ​(accept via ​b​a)=0.4⋅0.01⋅1=0.004,p_{\theta}(\text{accept via }a)=0.6\cdot 0.1=0.06,\qquad p_{\theta}(\text{accept via }ba)=0.4\cdot 0.01\cdot 1=0.004,

so pθ​(b∣τ⁡(y)∈L)=0.004/(0.06+0.004)≈0.0625≠0.4p_{\theta}(b\mid\tau(y)\in L)=0.004/(0.06+0.004)\approx 0.0625\neq 0.4. ∎

4 Formal State-Space Blowup from Nonterminal Delegation

4.1 Static control-state counts

Consider the canonical language L={an​bn:n≥0}L=\{a^{n}b^{n}:n\geq 0\} and grammars:

G1\displaystyle G_{1} :S→a​S​b|ε\displaystyle:S\to aSb\mid\varepsilon
G2\displaystyle G_{2} :S→aAb∣ε,A→aAb∣ε.\displaystyle:S\to aAb\mid\varepsilon,\quad A\to aAb\mid\varepsilon.

Both satisfy ℒ⁡(G1)=ℒ⁡(G2)=L\mathcal{L}(G_{1})=\mathcal{L}(G_{2})=L.

Definition 10 (Grammar size functional).

For a CFG G=(N,Σ,P,S)G=(N,\Sigma,P,S), define the right-hand-side length of p=(A→α)p=(A\to\alpha) as |α||\alpha|. Define the compilation control-state count

κ⁡(G)≔1+2​|N|+∑p∈P(|rhs⁡(p)|+1),\kappa(G)\coloneqq 1+2|N|+\sum_{p\in P}(|\mathrm{rhs}(p)|+1),

matching the construction in Definition 5.

Lemma 2 (Exact compiled control-state count).

For every CFG GG, the compiled NPDA 𝒜G\mathcal{A}_{G} has exactly κ⁡(G)\kappa(G) control states.

Proof.

By Definition 5, QQ contains: (i) one start state; (ii) two states per nonterminal (entry/exit); and (iii) for every production pp with RHS length mm, a dot-position chain of size m+1m+1. Summing yields κ⁡(G)\kappa(G). ∎

Lemma 3 (State-space blowup for G2G_{2} vs. G1G_{1}).

Under the compilation of Definition 5,

κ⁡(G1)=8,κ⁡(G2)=15.\kappa(G_{1})=8,\qquad\kappa(G_{2})=15.

In particular, κ⁡(G2)>κ⁡(G1)\kappa(G_{2})>\kappa(G_{1}) and the compiled control-state space inflates by a factor 15/815/8.

Proof.

For G1G_{1}: |N|=1|N|=1, productions S→a​S​bS\to aSb (RHS length 33) and S→εS\to\varepsilon (length 00):

κ⁡(G1)=1+2⋅1+((3+1)+(0+1))=8.\kappa(G_{1})=1+2\cdot 1+((3+1)+(0+1))=8.

For G2G_{2}: |N|=2|N|=2, four productions (two of length 33, two of length 00):

κ⁡(G2)=1+2⋅2+2⋅(3+1)+2⋅(0+1)=15.\kappa(G_{2})=1+2\cdot 2+2\cdot(3+1)+2\cdot(0+1)=15.

∎

4.2 Online consequences for masking engines

Definition 11 (Bitset-style active-set engine).

An active-set engine represents the set of live control states as a bitset over QQ, and updates the bitset by applying precomputed adjacency lists for ε\varepsilon-moves and terminal moves.

Proposition 3 (Lower bound induced by control-state inflation).

Fix any bitset-style active-set engine and any grammar GG. If the engine performs any operation that scans the entire bitset universe once per decoding step (e.g., to compute ε\varepsilon-closure, normalize, or garbage-collect inactive states), then the per-step overhead is Ω⁡(κ⁡(G))\Omega(\kappa(G)). Consequently, replacing G1G_{1} by G2G_{2} increases that overhead by a multiplicative factor of at least 15/815/8.

Proof.

Scanning a bitset of length κ⁡(G)\kappa(G) costs Ω⁡(κ⁡(G))\Omega(\kappa(G)) in the RAM model. The multiplicative factor follows from Lemma 3. ∎

Remark 3.

This is an engine-level statement about a common representation strategy, not a universal lower bound over all implementations. It isolates a checkable invariant: redundant nonterminal structure enlarges the compiled state universe, increases memory footprint, and typically worsens cache locality, even when language acceptance is unchanged.

5 Structural Ambiguity Cost and Parse Forest Density

5.1 Two equivalent grammars for Σ∗\Sigma^{*}

Let Σ={a,b}\Sigma=\{a,b\}. Define:

G3\displaystyle G_{3} :S→a​S​∣b​S∣​ε,\displaystyle:S\to aS\mid bS\mid\varepsilon,
G4\displaystyle G_{4} :S0→S|ε,S→S​S​∣a∣​b.\displaystyle:S_{0}\to S\mid\varepsilon,\quad S\to SS\mid a\mid b.
Lemma 4 (Language equivalence).

ℒ⁡(G3)=ℒ⁡(G4)=Σ∗\mathcal{L}(G_{3})=\mathcal{L}(G_{4})=\Sigma^{*}.

Proof.

G3G_{3} generates any string by repeatedly emitting aa or bb before terminating with the ε\varepsilon case; thus ℒ⁡(G3)=Σ∗\mathcal{L}(G_{3})=\Sigma^{*}. In G4G_{4}, SS generates all nonempty strings via S→aS\to a, S→bS\to b, and closure under S→S​SS\to SS, while S0S_{0} additionally permits the empty string. Thus ℒ⁡(G4)=Σ∗\mathcal{L}(G_{4})=\Sigma^{*}. ∎

Remark 4.

The use of the auxiliary start symbol S0S_{0} in G4G_{4} avoids spurious ε\varepsilon-expansion ambiguity that arises when ε\varepsilon is directly permitted by the recursive nonterminal SS (which would yield infinitely many derivations for the empty string).

5.2 Parse trees and Catalan ambiguity

Definition 12 (Parse-tree count).

For a grammar GG and string w∈Σ∗w\in\Sigma^{*}, let AG​(w)≔|PTG​(w)|A_{G}(w)\coloneqq|\mathrm{PT}_{G}(w)| denote the number of distinct parse trees deriving ww from the start symbol.

Lemma 5 (Catalan parse explosion for G4G_{4}).

For any nonempty w∈{a,b}nw\in\{a,b\}^{n} with n≥1n\geq 1,

AG4​(w)=Cn−1,A_{G_{4}}(w)=C_{n-1},

where CkC_{k} is the kk-th Catalan number, and AG4​(w)A_{G_{4}}(w) is therefore exponential in nn.

Proof.

In G4G_{4}, every terminal is produced by a leaf rule (S→aS\to a or S→bS\to b). Thus any parse tree for a string of length n≥1n\geq 1 is a full binary tree with nn leaves, whose internal nodes are applications of S→S​SS\to SS. The leaf labels are forced by ww. Therefore AG4​(w)A_{G_{4}}(w) equals the number of full binary trees with nn leaves, which is Cn−1C_{n-1}. ∎

5.3 Packed-forest density

We use half-open spans [i,j)[i,j) on positions 0,1,…,n0,1,\dots,n.

Definition 13 (Packed-forest split count).

In the natural SPPF-style representation for G4G_{4} [29, 17], a symbol node S⁡[i,j]S[i,j] exists for each span derivable by SS, and a packed node records each distinct split S⁡[i,j]⇒S⁡[i,k]​S​[k,j]S[i,j]\Rightarrow S[i,k]\,S[k,j] with i<k<ji<k<j.

Lemma 6 (Tight packed-forest size for G4G_{4}).

Fix any nonempty w∈{a,b}nw\in\{a,b\}^{n} with n≥2n\geq 2. The number of symbol nodes for SS is (n+12)=Θ⁡(n2)\binom{n+1}{2}=\Theta(n^{2}), and the total number of packed nodes is

Pn=∑0≤i<j≤n(j−i−1)=(n+13)=Θ⁡(n3).P_{n}=\sum_{0\leq i<j\leq n}(j-i-1)=\binom{n+1}{3}=\Theta(n^{3}).
Proof.

A symbol node S⁡[i,j]S[i,j] exists for every 0≤i<j≤n0\leq i<j\leq n because SS derives any nonempty substring, giving (n+12)\binom{n+1}{2} symbol nodes. For a fixed span [i,j)[i,j) of length L≥2L\geq 2, rule S→S​SS\to SS can split at any k∈(i,j)k\in(i,j), yielding L−1=(j−i−1)L-1=(j-i-1) packed nodes. Summing over all spans,

Pn=∑0≤i<j≤n(j−i−1).P_{n}=\sum_{0\leq i<j\leq n}(j-i-1).

The triple (i,k,j)(i,k,j) with 0≤i<k<j≤n0\leq i<k<j\leq n is in bijection with a 3-element subset of {0,…,n}\{0,\dots,n\}, so Pn=(n+13)P_{n}=\binom{n+1}{3}. ∎

5.4 Structural ambiguity cost

Definition 14 (Structural ambiguity cost (SAC)).

Fix a grammar GG and an online strategy maintaining a packed structure FtF_{t} for the length-tt prefix of ww. Define the per-step increment

ΔG​(t,w)≔|Ft​(w)|−|Ft−1​(w)|,\Delta_{G}(t;w)\coloneqq|F_{t}(w)|-|F_{t-1}(w)|,

and the worst-case structural ambiguity cost

SACG​(t)≔maxw∈Σt⁡ΔG​(t,w).\mathrm{SAC}_{G}(t)\coloneqq\max_{w\in\Sigma^{t}}\Delta_{G}(t;w).
Theorem 2 (SAC separation: G3G_{3} vs. G4G_{4}).

For G4G_{4}, SACG4​(t)=Θ⁡(t2)\mathrm{SAC}_{G_{4}}(t)=\Theta(t^{2}). For G3G_{3}, there exists a deterministic online strategy achieving SACG3​(t)=O​(1)\mathrm{SAC}_{G_{3}}(t)=O(1).

Proof.

For G4G_{4}, when the tt-th symbol arrives, all new spans [i,t)[i,t) for 0≤i<t0\leq i<t become available. Each span [i,t)[i,t) of length t−i≥2t-i\geq 2 admits (t−i−1)(t-i-1) new binary splits. The total number of newly introduced packed alternatives is

∑i=0t−2(t−i−1)=∑m=1t−1m=t⁡(t−1)2=Ω⁡(t2).\sum_{i=0}^{t-2}(t-i-1)=\sum_{m=1}^{t-1}m=\frac{t(t-1)}{2}=\Omega(t^{2}).

Lemma 6 provides a matching O⁡(t2)O(t^{2}) upper bound on new packed nodes at step tt, so SACG4​(t)=Θ⁡(t2)\mathrm{SAC}_{G_{4}}(t)=\Theta(t^{2}).

For G3G_{3}, the grammar is right-linear (hence regular) and unambiguous; an online strategy need only track the current unambiguous state, which is constant-sized. Thus SACG3​(t)=O​(1)\mathrm{SAC}_{G_{3}}(t)=O(1). ∎

Corollary 1 (Cumulative online cost).

For G4G_{4}, cumulative packed-structure growth over a length-nn string is Θ⁡(n3)\Theta(n^{3}). For G3G_{3}, cumulative cost is O⁡(n)O(n).

Proof.

Summing Θ⁡(t2)\Theta(t^{2}) over t=1,…,nt=1,\dots,n yields Θ⁡(n3)\Theta(n^{3}); Lemma 6 provides the matching upper bound. For G3G_{3}, summing O⁡(1)O(1) gives O⁡(n)O(n). ∎

Remark 5 (A stress test for engines, not for the language).

For Σ∗\Sigma^{*}, the ideal admissibility oracle is trivial: all tokens are always admissible and ⟨eos⟩\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle is always admissible. Nevertheless, when the grammar engine is treated as a black-box CFG executor, internal ambiguity can force it to maintain large packed structures merely to rediscover this trivial oracle. SAC quantifies that overhead.

6 Engine-Independent Lower Bounds for Parse-Preserving Masking

This section elevates the SAC analysis into an engine-independent lower bound by formalizing a broad class of engines that are simultaneously (i) sound for masking and (ii) parse-preserving in a retrieval-efficient sense.

6.1 A parse-preserving masking model

Definition 15 (Online masking engine).

An online CFG masking engine for grammar GG is an algorithm that, after reading each prefix u∈Σ∗u\in\Sigma^{*}, outputs ΩG​(u)\Omega_{G}(u) and updates an internal state σ⁡(u)\sigma(u) used for subsequent steps.

Definition 16 (Parse-preserving, retrieval-efficient engine).

Fix a grammar GG and a prefix uu. Let 𝒫G​(u)\mathcal{P}_{G}(u) denote the set of all partial parse structures consistent with uu (i.e., all packed split alternatives that can appear in some parse forest for some completion of uu). An online engine is parse-preserving if σ⁡(u)\sigma(u) determines 𝒫G​(u)\mathcal{P}_{G}(u) exactly (there exists a deterministic extractor recovering 𝒫G​(u)\mathcal{P}_{G}(u) from σ⁡(u)\sigma(u)). It is retrieval-efficient if the extractor enumerates all elements of 𝒫G​(u)\mathcal{P}_{G}(u) in O​(|𝒫G​(u)|)O(|\mathcal{P}_{G}(u)|) time. This is the standard output-sensitive retrieval posture used in generalized parsing [29, 17] and the retrieval-efficient parsing model studied in [18].

Remark 6 (Why retrieval efficiency is principled).

Without a retrieval requirement, an engine could vacuously “preserve all parses” by storing the pair (G,u)(G,u) and recomputing parse information on demand. Retrieval efficiency rules out this degenerate loophole by requiring that the maintained state genuinely encodes the parse set in an output-sensitive way.

6.2 The universal Ω⁡(t2)\Omega(t^{2}) per-token lower bound

Theorem 3 (Engine-independent SAC lower bound).

There exists a constant-size CFG G⋆G^{\star} and a family of prefixes of length tt such that any online masking engine that is both sound and parse-preserving retrieval-efficient for G⋆G^{\star} must incur Ω⁡(t2)\Omega(t^{2}) per-token update work in the worst case. The cumulative work over a length-nn input is therefore Ω⁡(n3)\Omega(n^{3}).

Proof.

Take G⋆=G4G^{\star}=G_{4}. Consider any length-tt prefix uu over {a,b}\{a,b\}. By Lemma 6, the set 𝒫G⋆​(u)\mathcal{P}_{G^{\star}}(u) contains all triples (i,k,j)(i,k,j) with 0≤i<k<j≤t0\leq i<k<j\leq t, with (t+13)\binom{t+1}{3} elements cumulatively. By the argument of Theorem 2, the number of triples newly introduced at step tt is (t2)=Ω⁡(t2)\binom{t}{2}=\Omega(t^{2}).

For a retrieval-efficient parse-preserving engine, σ(u1:t)\sigma(u_{1:t}) must permit enumeration of all elements of 𝒫G⋆(u1:t)\mathcal{P}_{G^{\star}}(u_{1:t}) in linear output time. Encoding Ω⁡(t2)\Omega(t^{2}) newly distinct objects requires Ω⁡(t2)\Omega(t^{2}) elementary memory writes in the RAM model; otherwise the extractor cannot enumerate them in O⁡(|𝒫|)O(|\mathcal{P}|) time. Thus the per-token update cost is Ω⁡(t2)\Omega(t^{2}), and summing gives Ω⁡(n3)\Omega(n^{3}). ∎

Remark 7 (Relation to classical parsing complexity).

Theorem 3 is unconditional within the specified semantic interface (soundness + retrieval-efficient parse preservation). It complements the classical results of Valiant [34] and Lee [18], which relate CFG parsing complexity to Boolean matrix multiplication via algorithmic reductions. Our argument is output-structure driven—grounded in the growth of the packed split set—rather than a reduction from another problem.

7 Decoding-Cost Equivalence Classes and Canonical Low-SAC Forms

Oracle invariance (Theorem 1) shows that language equivalence preserves the admissible token oracle. In this section we ask a finer question: when are two equivalent grammars also equivalent from the decoder’s cost perspective?

7.1 Intrinsic SAC

Definition 17 (Intrinsic parse-preserving SAC).

Fix a grammar GG. Let ℰpp​(G)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{pp}}(G) be the class of sound, retrieval-efficient parse-preserving online masking engines for GG. Define the intrinsic SAC as

SACG⋆​(t)≔infE∈ℰpp​(G)maxw∈Σt⁡ΔGE​(t,w),\mathrm{SAC}^{\star}_{G}(t)\coloneqq\inf_{E\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{pp}}(G)}\;\;\max_{w\in\Sigma^{t}}\Delta^{E}_{G}(t;w),

where ΔGE​(t,w)\Delta^{E}_{G}(t;w) is the engine-induced per-step growth of its maintained parse representation (measured in primitive parse objects).

Remark 8.

The infimum captures the best possible asymptotic behavior among engines that preserve all parses retrieval-efficiently. It abstracts away implementation details while remaining meaningfully constrained by Theorem 3.

7.2 Cost-equivalence relations

Definition 18 (Cost equivalence).

For grammars GG and HH over a shared terminal alphabet, define:

  • •

    Language equivalence: G≡LHG\equiv_{L}H iff ℒ⁡(G)=ℒ⁡(H)\mathcal{L}(G)=\mathcal{L}(H).

  • •

    SAC equivalence: G≡SACHG\equiv_{\mathrm{SAC}}H iff there exist constants c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0 and t0t_{0} such that for all t≥t0t\geq t_{0},

    c1​SACG⋆​(t)≤SACH⋆​(t)≤c2​SACG⋆​(t).c_{1}\,\mathrm{SAC}^{\star}_{G}(t)\leq\mathrm{SAC}^{\star}_{H}(t)\leq c_{2}\,\mathrm{SAC}^{\star}_{G}(t).
  • •

    Decoding-cost equivalence: G≡decHG\equiv_{\mathrm{dec}}H iff G≡LHG\equiv_{L}H and G≡SACHG\equiv_{\mathrm{SAC}}H.

Remark 9 (Interpretation).

G≡LHG\equiv_{L}H implies identical admissible token sets (Theorem 1). G≡decHG\equiv_{\mathrm{dec}}H strengthens this: the best possible parse-preserving online cost is asymptotically the same, so the grammars are equivalent not just semantically but from a decoder-cost perspective.

7.3 Canonical low-SAC representatives under bounded rewrites

Full minimization of pushdown models is NP-hard even in restricted settings [11], so any canonical minimal-SAC claim must be carefully scoped.

Definition 19 (Bounded rewrite family).

Fix a finite set of local grammar rewrites ℛ\mathcal{R}, each mapping a grammar to a language-equivalent grammar. For integer k≥0k\geq 0, let 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖼𝗁ℛ,k​(G)\mathsf{Reach}_{\mathcal{R},k}(G) be the finite set of grammars reachable from GG by applying at most kk rewrites from ℛ\mathcal{R}.

Theorem 4 (Existence of minimal-SAC representatives).

Fix ℛ,k\mathcal{R},k, and a grammar GG such that every rewrite in ℛ\mathcal{R} preserves ℒ⁡(G)\mathcal{L}(G). Then there exists Gmin∈𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖼𝗁ℛ,k​(G)G_{\min}\in\mathsf{Reach}_{\mathcal{R},k}(G) such that

SACGmin⋆​(t)≤SACH⋆​(t)for all ​H∈𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖼𝗁ℛ,k​(G)​ and all ​t.\mathrm{SAC}^{\star}_{G_{\min}}(t)\leq\mathrm{SAC}^{\star}_{H}(t)\quad\text{for all }H\in\mathsf{Reach}_{\mathcal{R},k}(G)\text{ and all }t.

Moreover, there exists such a GminG_{\min} that is also minimal for any finite tie-breaker functional (e.g., grammar size) over 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖼𝗁ℛ,k​(G)\mathsf{Reach}_{\mathcal{R},k}(G).

Proof.

𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖼𝗁ℛ,k​(G)\mathsf{Reach}_{\mathcal{R},k}(G) is finite since ℛ\mathcal{R} is finite and kk is bounded. The pointwise partial order induced by SAC⋆\mathrm{SAC}^{\star} over this finite set has at least one minimal element. Applying any finite tie-breaker selects a canonical representative. ∎

Remark 10 (Scope).

Theorem 4 is an existence result: a canonical low-SAC object is mathematically well-defined once one fixes a bounded transformation family. It does not assert computability of GminG_{\min} in general, nor that unrestricted global minimization is tractable.

8 Grammar-Conditioned Autoregressive Processes

We now move beyond parsing mechanics and treat constrained decoding as a stochastic process interacting with a formal language constraint. This develops the theoretical foundations that quantify the distortion introduced by hard masking relative to true conditional sampling.

8.1 True conditioning via a Doob hh-transform

Fix a base autoregressive model p⁡(⋅)p(\cdot) over token sequences terminated by ⟨eos⟩\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle. Let L⊆Σ∗L\subseteq\Sigma^{*} be the target language with acceptance event

E≔{τ(y1:T)∈L and yT=⟨eos⟩}.E\coloneqq\{\tau(y_{1:T})\in L\text{ and }y_{T}=\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle\}.
Definition 20 (Survival function).

For any prefix token sequence y<ty_{<t}, define the survival probability

h⁡(y<t)≔Prp⁡(E∣y<t).h(y_{<t})\coloneqq\Pr_{p}(E\mid y_{<t}).
Theorem 5 (Doob hh-transform for conditional decoding).

Assume h⁡(y<t)>0h(y_{<t})>0. Then the true conditional next-token distribution satisfies

pE​(v∣y<t)≔Prp⁡(yt=v∣y<t,E)=p⁡(v∣y<t)⋅h⁡(y<t​v)h⁡(y<t).p_{E}(v\mid y_{<t})\coloneqq\Pr_{p}(y_{t}=v\mid y_{<t},E)=p(v\mid y_{<t})\cdot\frac{h(y_{<t}v)}{h(y_{<t})}.
Proof.

By Bayes’ rule and the tower property,

Pr⁡(yt=v∣y<t,E)=Pr⁡(yt=v∣y<t)​Pr⁡(E∣y<t​v)h⁡(y<t)=p⁡(v∣y<t)​h⁡(y<t​v)h⁡(y<t).\Pr(y_{t}=v\mid y_{<t},E)=\frac{\Pr(y_{t}=v\mid y_{<t})\Pr(E\mid y_{<t}v)}{h(y_{<t})}=p(v\mid y_{<t})\frac{h(y_{<t}v)}{h(y_{<t})}.

This is the discrete-time analogue of Doob’s hh-transform for Markov chains [7, 20]. ∎

Definition 21 (Hard-masked process).

Let A⁡(y<t)≔ΩG​(τ⁡(y<t))A(y_{<t})\coloneqq\Omega_{G}(\tau(y_{<t})) be the admissible token set. Define the hard-masked next-token distribution

q⁡(v∣y<t)≔p(v∣y<t) 1[v∈A(y<t)]∑w∈A⁡(y<t)p⁡(w∣y<t).q(v\mid y_{<t})\coloneqq\frac{p(v\mid y_{<t})\,\mathbf{1}[v\in A(y_{<t})]}{\sum_{w\in A(y_{<t})}p(w\mid y_{<t})}.

8.2 Exact characterization and distortion bounds

Since h⁡(y<t​v)=0h(y_{<t}v)=0 whenever v∉A⁡(y<t)v\notin A(y_{<t}), both pEp_{E} and qq have support contained in A⁡(y<t)A(y_{<t}) when h⁡(y<t)>0h(y_{<t})>0. The distributions differ in how they weight admissible branches.

Theorem 6 (When hard masking equals true conditioning).

For a fixed prefix y<ty_{<t} with h⁡(y<t)>0h(y_{<t})>0, the following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    q(⋅∣y<t)=pE(⋅∣y<t)q(\cdot\mid y_{<t})=p_{E}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}),

  2. 2.

    h⁡(y<t​v)h(y_{<t}v) is constant over all admissible v∈A⁡(y<t)v\in A(y_{<t}).

Proof.

Restricting to A=A⁡(y<t)A=A(y_{<t}):

pE​(v∣y<t)∝p⁡(v∣y<t)​h​(y<t​v),q⁡(v∣y<t)∝p⁡(v∣y<t).p_{E}(v\mid y_{<t})\propto p(v\mid y_{<t})\,h(y_{<t}v),\qquad q(v\mid y_{<t})\propto p(v\mid y_{<t}).

These coincide iff the multiplicative factor h⁡(y<t​v)h(y_{<t}v) is constant over AA. ∎

Definition 22 (Survival spread).

For prefix y<ty_{<t} with admissible set A=A⁡(y<t)A=A(y_{<t}), define

hmin​(y<t)≔minv∈A⁡h⁡(y<t​v),hmax​(y<t)≔maxv∈A⁡h⁡(y<t​v),h_{\min}(y_{<t})\coloneqq\min_{v\in A}h(y_{<t}v),\qquad h_{\max}(y_{<t})\coloneqq\max_{v\in A}h(y_{<t}v),

and spread ratio Γ⁡(y<t)≔hmax​(y<t)/hmin​(y<t)\Gamma(y_{<t})\coloneqq h_{\max}(y_{<t})/h_{\min}(y_{<t}) (with Γ=∞\Gamma=\infty if hmin=0h_{\min}=0).

Proposition 4 (One-step KL bound).

Assume 0<hmin​(y<t)≤hmax​(y<t)<∞0<h_{\min}(y_{<t})\leq h_{\max}(y_{<t})<\infty. Then

KL(q(⋅∣y<t)∥pE(⋅∣y<t))≤logΓ(y<t).\operatorname{KL}\!\big(q(\cdot\mid y_{<t})\,\|\,p_{E}(\cdot\mid y_{<t})\big)\;\leq\;\log\Gamma(y_{<t}).
Proof.

Write A=A⁡(y<t)A=A(y_{<t}), pv=p⁡(v∣y<t)p_{v}=p(v\mid y_{<t}), hv=h⁡(y<t​v)h_{v}=h(y_{<t}v), Z=∑w∈ApwZ=\sum_{w\in A}p_{w}, H=∑w∈Apw​hwH=\sum_{w\in A}p_{w}h_{w}. Then qv=pv/Zq_{v}=p_{v}/Z and pvE=pv​hv/Hp^{E}_{v}=p_{v}h_{v}/H, giving

KL(q∥pE)=𝔼q[logqvpvE]=logHZ−𝔼q[loghv].\operatorname{KL}(q\|p_{E})=\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\left[\log\frac{q_{v}}{p^{E}_{v}}\right]=\log\frac{H}{Z}-\mathbb{E}_{q}[\log h_{v}].

Since hmin≤hv≤hmaxh_{\min}\leq h_{v}\leq h_{\max}, we have log⁡(H/Z)≤log⁡hmax\log(H/Z)\leq\log h_{\max} and −𝔼q​[log⁡hv]≤−log⁡hmin-\mathbb{E}_{q}[\log h_{v}]\leq-\log h_{\min}, so KL(q∥pE)≤loghmax−loghmin=logΓ(y<t)\operatorname{KL}(q\|p_{E})\leq\log h_{\max}-\log h_{\min}=\log\Gamma(y_{<t}). ∎

Corollary 2 (One-step total-variation bound).

Under the assumptions of Proposition 4,

TV(q(⋅∣y<t),pE(⋅∣y<t))≤12​log⁡Γ​(y<t).\operatorname{TV}\!\big(q(\cdot\mid y_{<t}),\,p_{E}(\cdot\mid y_{<t})\big)\;\leq\;\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\log\Gamma(y_{<t})}.
Proof.

Apply Pinsker’s inequality TV⁡(P,Q)≤KL(P∥Q)/2\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)\leq\sqrt{\operatorname{KL}(P\|Q)/2} to Proposition 4. ∎

Remark 11 (Interpretation).

Hard masking approximates true conditional sampling when survival probabilities from admissible next tokens are nearly equal (Γ⁡(y<t)≈1\Gamma(y_{<t})\approx 1). This formalizes the intuition that hard masking ignores “ease of completion” effects and quantifies distortion purely in terms of completion-probability variability. The spread Γ\Gamma is large when different admissible tokens lead to vastly different probabilities of eventual acceptance, and small when the constraint is nearly uniform over admissible branches.

9 Neural Integration: Attention and Mixture-of-Experts Routing

We express the algebra by which a reachability oracle modulates logits in a Transformer and extend the formulation to MoE routing probabilities.

9.1 Transformer logits under grammar-modulated admissibility

Let a causal Transformer [35] compute a hidden state ht∈ℝdh_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} from prefix y<ty_{<t} (with KV-caching assumed). The unmasked logits are

ℓt=Wout​ht+bout∈ℝ|𝒱|.\ell_{t}=W_{\mathrm{out}}h_{t}+b_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}.

Let At≔ΩG​(τ⁡(y<t))A_{t}\coloneqq\Omega_{G}(\tau(y_{<t})) denote the admissible token set. The masked logits are

ℓt(G)≔ℓt+mAt,\ell_{t}^{(G)}\coloneqq\ell_{t}+m_{A_{t}}, (2)

and the constrained next-token distribution is

qθG​(yt=v∣y<t)=softmax⁡(ℓt(G))​(v)=exp(ℓt(v))𝟏[v∈At]∑w∈Atexp⁡(ℓt​(w)).q_{\theta}^{G}(y_{t}=v\mid y_{<t})=\mathrm{softmax}(\ell_{t}^{(G)})(v)=\frac{\exp(\ell_{t}(v))\mathbf{1}[v\in A_{t}]}{\sum_{w\in A_{t}}\exp(\ell_{t}(w))}. (3)

This is the algebraic logit modulation performed by GCD engines [28, 2, 23, 6, 33].

9.2 MoE routing under grammar state

Consider a Transformer with MoE feed-forward blocks [30, 10]. At layer ℓ\ell and position tt, the gating network produces pre-activations gt,ℓ∈ℝEg_{t,\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{E} over EE experts. Standard routing computes

rt,ℓ=softmax⁡(gt,ℓ),ℰt,ℓ=TopK⁡(rt,ℓ),ht,ℓ′=∑e∈ℰt,ℓαt,ℓ,e​FFNe​(ht,ℓ),r_{t,\ell}=\mathrm{softmax}(g_{t,\ell}),\qquad\mathcal{E}_{t,\ell}=\mathrm{TopK}(r_{t,\ell}),\qquad h^{\prime}_{t,\ell}=\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{t,\ell}}\alpha_{t,\ell,e}\,\mathrm{FFN}_{e}(h_{t,\ell}),

with normalized weights αt,ℓ,e\alpha_{t,\ell,e}. Let 𝒞t≔CoReachG⁡(τ⁡(y<t))\mathcal{C}_{t}\coloneqq\operatorname{CoReach}_{G}(\tau(y_{<t})) denote the live configuration set. A grammar-aware MoE can incorporate 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} via a feature embedding ϕ⁡(𝒞t)∈ℝk\phi(\mathcal{C}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{k}:

rt,ℓ(G)=softmax⁡(gt,ℓ+Uℓ​ϕ​(𝒞t)),r_{t,\ell}^{(G)}\;=\;\mathrm{softmax}\!\big(g_{t,\ell}+U_{\ell}\,\phi(\mathcal{C}_{t})\big), (4)

where Uℓ∈ℝE×kU_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times k} is learned. This defines a joint constraint coupling syntactic state to conditional computation.

9.3 Latency envelopes

Let V≔|𝒱|V\coloneqq|\mathcal{V}| (vocabulary size), BB beam width, tt the current step, ℓ¯≔𝔼⁡[|τ⁡(yt)|]\bar{\ell}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[|\tau(y_{t})|] the average terminal-length per token, MtM_{t} the live-configuration representation size per hypothesis, and Kt≔|ΩG​(τ⁡(y<t))|K_{t}\coloneqq|\Omega_{G}(\tau(y_{<t}))| the number of admissible tokens.

Definition 23 (Abstract engine-step primitives).

Let UpdateG​(Mt,ℓ¯)\mathrm{Update}_{G}(M_{t},\bar{\ell}) be the cost to update the grammar engine state after consuming one token, and EnumerateG​(Mt)\mathrm{Enumerate}_{G}(M_{t}) be the cost to enumerate admissible tokens.

Proposition 5 (Per-step complexity: dense-vocabulary masking).

If the model computes dense logits over all VV tokens for each of BB hypotheses, the per-step time is

O⁡(B⋅(Tmodel​(t)+UpdateG​(Mt,ℓ¯)+EnumerateG​(Mt)+V)),O\!\big(B\cdot\big(T_{\mathrm{model}}(t)+\mathrm{Update}_{G}(M_{t},\bar{\ell})+\mathrm{Enumerate}_{G}(M_{t})+V\big)\big),

where Tmodel​(t)T_{\mathrm{model}}(t) is the Transformer forward cost under KV-caching.

Proof.

Per hypothesis: compute logits (Tmodel​(t)T_{\mathrm{model}}(t)), update and enumerate mask (UpdateG+EnumerateG\mathrm{Update}_{G}+\mathrm{Enumerate}_{G}), then scan a VV-length mask. Multiply by BB. ∎

Proposition 6 (Per-step complexity: sparse admissible-set scoring).

If the inference stack scores only admissible tokens (e.g., via trie-restricted projection), then the VV term may be replaced by KtK_{t}:

O⁡(B⋅(Tmodel​(t)+UpdateG​(Mt,ℓ¯)+EnumerateG​(Mt)+Kt)).O\!\big(B\cdot\big(T_{\mathrm{model}}(t)+\mathrm{Update}_{G}(M_{t},\bar{\ell})+\mathrm{Enumerate}_{G}(M_{t})+K_{t}\big)\big).
Corollary 3 (SAC-induced masking bottleneck).

For G4G_{4} and a sound packed-structure engine, Mt=Ω⁡(t2)M_{t}=\Omega(t^{2}) (Theorem 3), so any update routine that touches newly created packed structure satisfies UpdateG4​(Mt,ℓ¯)=Ω⁡(t2)\mathrm{Update}_{G_{4}}(M_{t},\bar{\ell})=\Omega(t^{2}). For G3G_{3}, one can maintain Mt=O⁡(1)M_{t}=O(1) giving UpdateG3=O⁡(1)\mathrm{Update}_{G_{3}}=O(1).

9.4 Grammar-conditioned logits with sound masking

Definition 24 (Grammar-conditioned logits).

Let et=ψ⁡(𝒞t)∈ℝke_{t}=\psi(\mathcal{C}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{k} embed the live configuration set. Define

ℓ~t​(v)≔ℓt​(v)+u​(v)⊤​et\tilde{\ell}_{t}(v)\coloneqq\ell_{t}(v)+u(v)^{\top}e_{t}

for learned vectors u⁡(v)∈ℝku(v)\in\mathbb{R}^{k}. Apply hard masking with AtA_{t}:

qθG,ψ​(v∣y<t)≔softmax⁡(ℓ~t+mAt)​(v).q_{\theta}^{G,\psi}(v\mid y_{<t})\coloneqq\mathrm{softmax}(\tilde{\ell}_{t}+m_{A_{t}})(v).
Proposition 7 (Soundness under grammar-conditioned logits).

Sampling from qθG,ψq_{\theta}^{G,\psi} yields only strings in ℒ⁡(G)\mathcal{L}(G) upon termination, for any embedding ψ\psi and weights u⁡(⋅)u(\cdot).

Proof.

The support of qθG,ψq_{\theta}^{G,\psi} is contained in AtA_{t} at every step by construction of hard masking. The argument of Proposition 2 applies unchanged. ∎

Remark 12.

Hard masking ensures correctness, while grammar-conditioned logits can reduce the frequency with which the mask truncates high-probability mass—a key distortion concern quantified by Proposition 4. In MoE models, the same embedding ete_{t} can be fed into the router via (4) to encourage expert specialization by syntactic region. Empirical validation requires controlled ablations on structured benchmarks such as JSONSchemaBench [12].

10 From SAC to Runtime Prediction, Grammar Optimization, and Hybrid Control

This section extends the SAC analysis into (i) an empirically calibratable performance model, (ii) an equivalence-preserving grammar optimizer, and (iii) deeper symbolic–neural coupling via instrumented engines.

10.1 Instrumented engines and SAC proxies

Production engines do not expose |Ft​(w)||F_{t}(w)| directly; they expose engine-native structures (Earley items, LR items, trie nodes, persistent-stack nodes, etc.). LLGuidance uses an Earley-based recognizer combined with token-trie traversal [15]; XGrammar employs vocabulary splitting and persistent-stack representations [6]. We introduce a general instrumentation interface to unify these.

Definition 25 (Instrumented decoding engine).

Fix grammar GG and tokenizer τ\tau. An instrumented decoding engine is a triple E=(Step,Mask,Ctr)E=(\mathrm{Step},\mathrm{Mask},\mathrm{Ctr}) where at each step tt:

  • •

    Step\mathrm{Step} advances engine state for each hypothesis;

  • •

    Mask\mathrm{Mask} returns ΩG​(τ⁡(y<t))\Omega_{G}(\tau(y_{<t}));

  • •

    Ctr\mathrm{Ctr} returns a vector of nonneg. counters recording symbolic work (items created, edges traversed, trie nodes visited, stack nodes touched, etc.).

Definition 26 (SAC proxy).

Let ct​(E,w)∈ℝ≥0dc_{t}(E;w)\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d} be the counter vector at step tt. A scalar SAC proxy is

StE​(w)≔⟨α,ct​(E,w)⟩S_{t}^{E}(w)\coloneqq\langle\alpha,c_{t}(E;w)\rangle

for some fixed α∈ℝ≥0d\alpha\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d}, chosen to estimate marginal per-step symbolic work.

Lemma 7 (Proxy lower-bounds SAC under split completeness).

Consider G4G_{4} with rule S→S​SS\to SS. Assume engine EE is split-complete: for every span [i,t)[i,t) of length ≥2\geq 2 in its maintained structure, it represents each split point kk with i<k<ti<k<t. Then there exists β>0\beta>0 such that for all tt,

maxw∈Σt⁡StE​(w)≥β⋅SACG4​(t).\max_{w\in\Sigma^{t}}S_{t}^{E}(w)\;\geq\;\beta\cdot\mathrm{SAC}_{G_{4}}(t).
Proof.

At step tt, split completeness forces the engine to account for each newly introduced split alternative for each new span ending at tt. By Theorem 2, this is Ω⁡(t2)\Omega(t^{2}) in the worst case. Any proxy assigning positive weight to such alternatives yields a linear lower bound on that count up to a constant. ∎

10.2 A predictive performance model

Let TNN​(t)T_{\mathrm{NN}}(t) denote GPU model forward time per hypothesis under KV-cache, and Tmask​(t)T_{\mathrm{mask}}(t) the CPU-side (or mixed) engine time for state advancement and mask computation.

Definition 27 (Critical-path step time).

Under ideal overlap,

Tstep​(t)≔max⁡{TNN​(t),Tmask​(t)}+Tsync​(t)+Tsel​(t),T_{\mathrm{step}}(t)\coloneqq\max\{T_{\mathrm{NN}}(t),\,T_{\mathrm{mask}}(t)\}+T_{\mathrm{sync}}(t)+T_{\mathrm{sel}}(t),

where Tsync​(t)T_{\mathrm{sync}}(t) accounts for synchronization and Tsel​(t)T_{\mathrm{sel}}(t) accounts for sampling/top-kk selection.

XGrammar explicitly targets “overlap grammar computation with GPU execution” as a latency optimization strategy [6]. A practical study should measure overlap and identify when masking becomes the critical path; Nsight Systems provides NVTX range annotations and timeline visualization for this purpose [22].

Definition 28 (Affine proxy-to-time model).

An affine proxy model is

Tmask​(t)≈a⋅StE​(w)+b,T_{\mathrm{mask}}(t)\approx a\cdot S_{t}^{E}(w)+b,

for constants a≥0a\geq 0, b≥0b\geq 0 estimated from empirical traces via, e.g., least-squares fit.

Remark 13 (Calibration toolchain).

Calibration is naturally performed on mask-only workloads (e.g., MaskBench) [14]. A complete toolchain combines: Nsight Systems for timeline/overlap analysis [22]; Linux perf for CPU PMU counters [24]; Nsight Compute for GPU cache/memory analysis [21]; PyTorch Profiler for operator-level attribution [25]; and CUDA allocator snapshots for memory pressure [26].

Proposition 8 (Beam amplification of symbolic work).

Assuming beam hypotheses do not share grammar engine state,

St,totalE=∑i=1BStE​(w(i))=Θ⁡(B⋅S¯t),S^{E}_{t,\mathrm{total}}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{B}S^{E}_{t}(w^{(i)})\;=\;\Theta(B\cdot\overline{S}_{t}),

where S¯t\overline{S}_{t} is the average proxy per hypothesis. Under the affine model, Tmask,total​(t)≈a⋅Θ⁡(B⋅S¯t)+b′T_{\mathrm{mask,total}}(t)\approx a\cdot\Theta(B\cdot\overline{S}_{t})+b^{\prime}.

Proof.

Counters are generated by disjoint engine updates; the proxy is additive across independent hypotheses. Substituting into the affine model absorbs constant terms into b′b^{\prime}. ∎

Remark 14 (DPDA compilation and batch efficiency).

When nondeterminism forces persistent-stack branching, StES_{t}^{E} can grow with beam even at fixed prefix length. Pre3 targets this by compiling LR(1) structures to a DPDA and precomputing prefix-conditioned edges to reduce runtime path exploration [5]. Within our framework this corresponds to reducing active configuration fanout and shrinking variance in StES_{t}^{E} across steps.

10.3 Automated grammar optimization

Oracle invariance (Theorem 1) permits a compiler searching over equivalent grammars to minimize an engine-dependent cost model.

Definition 29 (Grammar optimization problem).

Fix engine family EE, tokenizer τ\tau, and workload 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Define the feasible set 𝒢⁡(G)≔{G′:ℒ⁡(G′)=ℒ⁡(G)}\mathcal{G}(G)\coloneqq\{G^{\prime}:\mathcal{L}(G^{\prime})=\mathcal{L}(G)\} and objective

minG′∈𝒢⁡(G)⁡𝔼w∼𝒟​[CostE​(G′,τ,w)],\min_{G^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}(G)}\;\;\mathbb{E}_{w\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\mathrm{Cost}_{E}(G^{\prime},\tau;w)\Big],

where CostE\mathrm{Cost}_{E} can combine static terms (e.g., κ⁡(G′)\kappa(G^{\prime})), dynamic terms (expected SAC proxy), and tokenizer alignment overhead.

Remark 15 (Tokenizer alignment).

DOMINO highlights that improper alignment between subword vocabularies and grammar terminals can distort model distributions and incur “bridge” handling overhead [2]. Park et al. formalize lexer-state-dependent token-to-terminal mapping to avoid inefficient combinations at runtime [23]. Thus misalignment cost is a first-class component of CostE\mathrm{Cost}_{E}.

Definition 30 (Inlining rewrite).

Let A∈NA\in N have productions A→γ1​∣⋯∣​γmA\to\gamma_{1}\mid\cdots\mid\gamma_{m}. An inlining rewrite replaces a production B→α​A​βB\to\alpha A\beta by the set {B→αγiβ:i=1,…,m}\{B\to\alpha\gamma_{i}\beta:i=1,\dots,m\}, leaving other productions unchanged.

Lemma 8 (Inlining preserves the language).

Assume AA is not the start symbol and the inlining rewrite introduces no new nonterminals. Then the rewritten grammar G′G^{\prime} satisfies ℒ⁡(G′)=ℒ⁡(G)\mathcal{L}(G^{\prime})=\mathcal{L}(G).

Proof.

Each derivation in GG applying B→α​A​βB\to\alpha A\beta followed by A⇒∗γiA\Rightarrow^{*}\gamma_{i} maps to a derivation in G′G^{\prime} using B→α​γi​βB\to\alpha\gamma_{i}\beta; thus ℒ⁡(G)⊆ℒ⁡(G′)\mathcal{L}(G)\subseteq\mathcal{L}(G^{\prime}). The reverse containment is symmetric. ∎

Remark 16 (Equality saturation for grammar optimization).

Even with local rewrites, the search space of equivalent grammars is large. Equality saturation with e-graphs [32, 37] offers a principled approach: represent grammar fragments in an e-graph, apply equivalence-preserving rewrites (inlining, delegation elimination, recursion normalization), attach cost analyses estimating κ\kappa, SAC proxy surrogates, and tokenizer alignment, then extract the minimum-cost equivalent grammar. Hardness results (NP-completeness of VPA minimization [11]) motivate heuristic or class-restricted optimization rather than global optimality.

11 Related Work

Parsing theory and reachability.

Classic CFG parsing algorithms provide the backbone for our formalization [9, 38]. GLR parsing and ambiguity complexity are developed in [17], and SPPF-based packed forest representations in [29]. Valiant’s reduction of CFG recognition to Boolean matrix multiplication [34] and Lee’s converse reduction [18] establish tight connections between general CFG parsing complexity and matrix multiplication; our engine-independent lower bounds (Section 6) are complementary and output-structure driven. CFL reachability and pushdown model checking are developed in [27, 4, 1].

Grammar-constrained decoding.

PICARD uses incremental parsing to reject invalid subword tokens during decoding [28]. DOMINO emphasizes subword-aligned constraining and non-invasive masking [2]. Park et al. analyze preprocessing/online tradeoffs and lexer-state-dependent token mapping [23]. XGrammar introduces vocabulary splitting, persistent stacks, grammar transformations, and CPU/GPU overlap [6]. SynCode provides a completeness/soundness framing [33]. Pre3 compiles deterministic pushdown automata to reduce runtime path exploration in large-batch settings [5]. JSONSchemaBench provides a large-scale structured-output benchmark with a MaskBench component isolating mask computation performance [12, 14]. Libraries such as Guidance, Outlines, and LLGuidance provide widely used constraint interfaces [19, 13, 8, 15].

Stochastic processes and hh-transforms.

The theory of Doob hh-transforms characterizes conditional Markov processes and bridges probabilistic analysis with harmonic function theory [7, 20]. Our use of the hh-transform to characterize GCD as true conditional decoding (Section 8) connects constrained generation to the classical theory of conditioning on rare events.

Grammar optimization.

Equality saturation and e-graphs [32, 37] provide a principled framework for optimization under equivalence, which we propose as a basis for automated grammar refactoring. NP-completeness of visibly pushdown automaton minimization [11] motivates heuristic and class-restricted approaches.

Neural architecture coupling.

The Transformer [35] and MoE architectures [30, 10] are the inference targets for our neural integration results. Constrained generation in semantic parsing is studied in [31], and LMQL provides a programming interface over constrained LLM decoding [3].

12 Conclusion

We formalized grammar-constrained decoding as a coupling between a neural next-token model and a pushdown reachability oracle derived from a CFG. Our contributions are as follows.

Oracle invariance (Theorem 1): language-equivalent grammars induce identical admissible token sets, hence identical logit masks, for every prefix. This invariance coexists with provable differences in engine state-space size and online update cost.

State-space blowup (Lemma 3): for the an​bna^{n}b^{n} language, we gave exact control-state counts under a concrete PDA compilation and showed a 15/815/8 blowup factor from redundant nonterminal delegation.

SAC bounds (Theorem 2, Corollary 1): concatenation grammars incur Θ⁡(t2)\Theta(t^{2}) incremental packed-structure growth and Θ⁡(n3)\Theta(n^{3}) cumulative cost; right-recursive grammars admit O⁡(1)O(1) and O⁡(n)O(n), respectively.

Engine-independent lower bounds (Theorem 3): any sound, retrieval-efficient, parse-preserving masking engine must incur Ω⁡(t2)\Omega(t^{2}) per-token work on G4G_{4}, making the SAC lower bound unconditional within this model.

Decoding-cost equivalence classes (Theorem 4): minimal-SAC grammar representatives exist within any bounded-rewrite family, providing a mathematically precise notion of canonical low-SAC normal forms.

Grammar-conditioned processes (Theorem 5, Proposition 4, Corollary 2): the true conditional sampler is characterized by a Doob hh-transform, and hard masking incurs a one-step KL distortion bounded by log⁡Γ⁡(y<t)\log\Gamma(y_{<t}), where Γ\Gamma measures survival-probability spread among admissible next tokens.

Neural integration and performance modeling: we derived latency envelopes for Transformer and MoE architectures, showed that SAC-induced bottlenecks affect masking-critical-path time under beam search, and connected these results to instrumentation-based predictive models and automated grammar optimization via equivalence-preserving rewrites and equality saturation [12, 5, 32, 37].

Together, these results establish a rigorous theoretical foundation for grammar refactoring as a latency optimization problem with well-defined semantic invariants and measurable cost surrogates.
